title: Room and Bell
premise: Marguerite Voss, a forensic property surveyor, is hired to appraise her late grandmother's house on Vellum Lane, where every photograph now contains an extra empty chair and the well in the back garden is filling itself with water that reflects rooms no one has built. The house was never haunted; it was rented — decades ago, her grandmother invited something in to save Marguerite's dying mother, and the lease is coming due. As the night stretches toward sunrise, Marguerite must choose between paying the debt herself, passing it to the child she didn't know she was carrying, or burning the truth out of the house entirely, knowing the fire will take every memory of the people she loved with it.
about_author: G. M. Marchetti is a former building inspector who spent eleven years cataloguing condemned properties across the Rust Belt before turning to fiction full-time. They write horror about structures that remember, and live in a farmhouse they refuse to have appraised.

chapters.title: The Commission
chapters.summary: Third-person limited, Marguerite's POV. A bank hires Marguerite to survey a probate property: her estranged grandmother's house, inherited by default. She takes it for the fee, telling herself family means nothing. Emotional beat: professional detachment established as armor, already cracking at the name on the deed.

chapters.title: Vellum Lane
chapters.summary: Marguerite arrives at the house at dusk, finding it immaculate inside despite nine months vacant — dust settled everywhere except the kitchen table, which bears four place settings. Beat: unease disguised as observation; her surveyor's instinct registers wrongness as measurement error.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Wrongs
chapters.summary: She catalogs anomalies like defects: clocks all stopped at 3:12, doors that open onto slightly different hallways than they closed from. POV stays tight and rational. Beat: competence as coping mechanism, the reader seeing what she refuses to.

chapters.title: The Extra Chair
chapters.summary: Going through photo albums for the estate file, Marguerite finds every family photograph now includes an empty wooden chair positioned just behind the subjects — including photos taken in other houses, other decades. Beat: first true fear, contained in a single held breath.

chapters.title: Grandmother's Ledger
chapters.summary: In the study safe she finds a ledger of payments — dates, amounts, and a recurring entry: 'RENT, PAID IN FULL' signed with her grandmother's initials, last dated the week of her death. Beat: dread reframed as mystery; she chooses investigation over flight.

chapters.title: Well Water
chapters.summary: The backyard well, capped since her childhood, stands open and brimming. The water shows reflections of lit windows in a house that isn't there. She drops a pebble; it never lands. Beat: the supernatural becomes undeniable, and she gets angry instead of afraid.

chapters.title: Phone Down
chapters.summary: Her calls won't connect; texts send but receive replies hours old, from numbers including her mother's, dead six years. One message reads 'don't sign anything.' Beat: isolation sealed; the outside world recedes like a tide going out.

chapters.title: The Tenant's Terms
chapters.summary: Behind the wallpaper in the pantry she finds a contract written in her grandmother's hand, countersigned in something brown-black: one life preserved, one life owed, renewable each generation. Beat: exposition delivered as violation — the house has been listening to her read.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: Flashback chapter, grandmother Odile's POV, 1971. Her daughter drowning in fever, Odile opens the well and asks for help. Something answers politely. Beat: love as original sin; the reader understands the bargain before Marguerite does.

chapters.title: Room 3:12
chapters.summary: Marguerite finds a door that wasn't there behind the staircase, opening onto a room where the clocks are right and her mother sits waiting, warm and alive. Beat: temptation rendered tenderly; grief weaponized.

chapters.title: The Mother Who Waits
chapters.summary: Still flashback-adjacent, present-tense dream logic. Her mother explains the arrangement gently: the house keeps its tenants' beloveds 'in escrow.' All she must do is stay. Beat: the horror of comfort; Marguerite nearly sits down.

chapters.title: Appraisal
chapters.summary: Snapping awake at the kitchen table, Marguerite realizes hours passed and her hands wrote an appraisal valuing the house at exactly one life. Beat: the house negotiates through her own profession; autonomy eroding.

chapters.title: Neighbors
chapters.summary: A neighbor, Mrs. Adeyemi, appears at the fence line at 2 a.m., warning her not to answer anything that knocks. Her family sold their claim back in 1988 and paid 'the difference.' Beat: exposition through witness; hope introduced and immediately complicated.

chapters.title: The Difference
chapters.summary: Mrs. Adeyemi shows her scarred hands: those who buy out pay in memories. She cannot remember her son's face, only that she loved him. Beat: the theme crystallizes — survival always invoices someone.

chapters.title: Knocking
chapters.summary: Something knocks at every door simultaneously, then politely at only the front. It sounds like her grandmother. Marguerite counts to sunrise on her watch, which has begun running backward. Beat: siege begins; time itself joins the opposition.

chapters.title: Photographs, Continued
chapters.summary: New photographs are developing in the albums: images of tonight, of Marguerite reading the contract, of the chair moving closer to the camera in each successive frame. Beat: surveillance horror; the house is documenting her for its files.

chapters.title: Odile's Confession
chapters.summary: A letter hidden in the chimney flue: Odile admits she knew the debt would fall to Marguerite and chose her mother's life anyway, asking forgiveness in advance. Beat: anger at the dead; love and betrayal revealed as the same act.

chapters.title: The Well Refills
chapters.summary: At 4 a.m. the well overflows, water threading through the grass into the house, rising ankle-deep and warm. In it she sees the lit rooms again — furnished with her own future. Beat: deadline made physical; the house is flooding in to collect.

chapters.title: Drowning Rooms
chapters.summary: Wading through the house, she passes doorways showing scenes: her wedding that never happened, a child's bedroom, her mother's kitchen. Each room offers to be real if she'll only step in. Beat: peak temptation; duty versus desire made architectural.

chapters.title: The Child
chapters.summary: Alone in the nursery-that-isn't, Marguerite understands the second heartbeat she's felt all night isn't the house's — she's pregnant, and the contract's fine print names 'issue of the tenant.' Beat: devastating turn; the debt has been accruing interest in her body.

chapters.title: Renegotiation
chapters.summary: She confronts the presence directly, demanding terms. It appears as the chair, finally occupied by a shape almost like a person, and speaks in the voices of everyone she's lost. Beat: confrontation without resolution; the entity is bureaucratic, patient, almost kind.

chapters.title: Terms of Surrender
chapters.summary: It offers three options: her life, her child's, or her memories of everyone the house ever kept — her mother, grandmother, the whole lineage erased from her. Sunrise is the deadline. Beat: false clarity; three exits, all of them doors closing.

chapters.title: Mrs. Adeyemi's Bargain
chapters.summary: The neighbor returns, offering to co-sign the debt, splitting it — a trick that destroyed her own family. Marguerite refuses to make another person pay. Beat: moral center asserted; refusal as character.

chapters.title: Reading the Fine Print
chapters.summary: Surveyor's eye to the end: Marguerite rereads the contract and finds the flaw — the lease binds 'the household,' and a household requires consent from all living members. She never signed. Beat: hope through expertise; her profession becomes her weapon.

chapters.title: The House Objects
chapters.summary: The house fights back: walls lengthen, doors multiply, the water rises to her knees, and her mother's voice pleads from Room 3:12. Beat: climax pressure mounting; the house reveals desperation beneath its courtesy.

chapters.title: Mother's Voice
chapters.summary: In Room 3:12, her mother begs her to stay, and Marguerite realizes the thing wearing her mother doesn't know things only her mother knew — it learned her from the photographs. Beat: heartbreak and liberation in one stroke; the bait exposed as forgery.

chapters.title: Withdrawal of Consent
chapters.summary: Marguerite formally revokes consent on behalf of the household, invoking the surveyor's authority over the property line: the well, she declares, is a separate parcel. Beat: legalistic exorcism; absurdity weaponized against the ancient.

chapters.title: The Parcel Line
chapters.summary: She stakes the boundary with her survey equipment, chalk-lining a circle the water cannot cross. The house screams in settling timber. Beat: triumph's first taste, immediately undercut as the ground itself shifts to swallow the stakes.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: The contract's final clause surfaces: if unpaid at sunrise, the house keeps everything in escrow forever — her mother, her memories, the child's future. Five minutes to dawn. Beat: darkest hour; every option costs everything.

chapters.title: What Marguerite Pays
chapters.summary: She chooses a fourth path: she pays the difference herself — not her life, but her memory of her mother, freely given, which the contract never anticipated because no one surrenders it willingly. Beat: sacrifice redefined; love expressed as loss.

chapters.title: Whiteout
chapters.summary: The extraction: memories leaving like water down a drain, faces dissolving from photographs as the sun crests. She holds onto one thing by brute will — not a face, but the feeling of being loved. Beat: agonizing, transcendent; the price paid in full.

chapters.title: Empty House
chapters.summary: Sunrise. The water drains, the extra chair is gone, the photographs show ordinary families. The house is just a house, worth exactly its appraisal. Beat: hollow victory; silence where the haunting was.

chapters.title: Aftermath, Measured
chapters.summary: Days later, Marguerite files her report, recommends demolition, and can't explain why she cries at strangers who resemble no one she knows. Beat: grief without referent; survival's invoice arrives quietly.

chapters.title: The Feeling That Stays
chapters.summary: She visits the demolished lot and finds the ledger's final page blown against the fence: her grandmother's handwriting added after death — 'Thank you, little one.' She doesn't know who wrote it, but she believes it. Beat: love outlasting memory; the theme resolved.

chapters.title: Appointment Kept
chapters.summary: At a routine prenatal checkup, the ultrasound technician frowns, checks the monitor twice, and says everything looks perfect — there's just an echo on the image, like a small chair beside the baby. Beat: dread returns, transformed; ambiguity planted.

chapters.title: Vellum Lane, Revisited
chapters.summary: Final chapter, years later implied. Marguerite, holding her daughter's hand, walks past a new house built on the old lot. The daughter waves at someone in an upstairs window. Marguerite squeezes her hand and keeps walking. Beat: open-ended coda; some leases transfer, but so does love — and this time, they walk away together.
